About: Relativistic Momentum vs. Velocity

Source

Lecture
14 — Mass
Simulation
Simulation 1 — Momentum vs velocity (guided inquiry)
Concept
Relativistic momentum p = γm₀v grows linearly at low speed but diverges as v → c, unlike the classical p = m₀v.
Serves
Distinguish rest mass from relativistic energy–momentum; appreciate why rest mass is invariant (m₀ stays fixed, γ drives the divergence); construct the four-momentum (p is its spatial component).
Inquiry
Expected behaviour near v = 0? Near v = c? Effect of doubling the rest mass m₀?
Misconception
Encoded in the prediction choices: (i) momentum approaches a finite maximum at v = c; (ii) doubling m₀ leaves the curve unchanged.

Welcome toRelativistic momentum vs. velocity

Compare Newton's momentum with the momentum relativity assigns to the same particle, right up to the edge of the speed of light.

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

Guided Inquiry

1 · Momentum against speed

Here’s what you’re looking at. A particle of rest mass m₀ moves at speed v. The blue curve is the momentum relativity assigns it, and the grey dashed line is the Newtonian value m₀v. Speeds are in units of c, and the vertical scale is fixed so you can compare the two at any setting.

2 · A force that never stops

Let’s start with a thought experiment. In Newton’s mechanics a constant force gives constant acceleration, so a long enough push carries any particle past c. Relativity keeps dp/dt = F. So what do you think gives way?

Try it: drag the marker toward c. The curve leaves the top of the plot, but v never reaches the amber line.

3 · Why γ belongs there

Now for the why. Momentum conservation has to hold in every inertial frame. What do you think goes wrong if momentum is taken to be plain m₀v?

4 · Changing the rest mass

Let’s try a different knob. Rest mass m₀ is the same number in every frame. Double it, holding v fixed. What do you think happens to the momentum curve?

Check it yourself: read p at v = 0.6c, then drag m₀ to 2.0, and 0.750 becomes 1.50.

5 · How steeply it climbs

One last estimate. The shaded band is the momentum relativity adds beyond m₀v. Raise the speed from 0.45c to 0.90c — an exact doubling. Make a guess: by roughly what factor does momentum grow?

Now try it: set v = 0.45c and read p, then set v = 0.90c.

6 · Momentum has no ceiling

Let’s pull it all together. Because p = γm₀v and γ → ∞ as v → c, a steady force makes momentum climb without limit while the speed flattens against c. Replacing m₀v by γm₀v is forced rather than fitted: only γm₀v is conserved in every inertial frame. And that’s why accelerators quote beam energy rather than beam speed.

The Physics

Relativistic momentum vs. velocity · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim plots the momentum that relativity assigns to a particle of rest mass m0 against its speed v, next to Newton's m0v. It shows where the two agree, where they part, and what controls the difference.

What you'll learn

  • How relativistic momentum compares with Newton's m₀v over the whole range of speeds, up to c.
  • How to read the momentum, and the factor γ, off the plot for any speed and rest mass.
  • What the rest mass m₀ does to the curve, and what it leaves alone.
  • Why momentum takes this form, and what stays the same in every frame.
The plot's layout, drawn to its axes for m₀ = 1.0 (curves cut off at 0.9c).

What's on screen

  • Blue curve: the relativistic momentum p/c at each speed.
  • Grey dashed line: Newton's momentum m₀v.
  • Amber dashed line: the speed limit v = c.
  • Violet marker: your point, set by the v slider.
  • Controls panel: m₀, v, and the readout γ and p/c at your point. Hover the plot to read any other point.

Axes: v/c across (0 to 1), p/c up (0 to 10), both in units where c = 1.

See itPut your point at v = 0.3c with m₀ = 1.0. Watch for: the violet marker on the blue curve, and its readout.

03

Speed levels off, momentum does not

In Newton's mechanics momentum is just mass times speed:

So a steady push, which adds momentum at a steady rate (F = dp/dt), could take a particle past any speed. Relativity keeps F = dp/dt, so something else has to give way.

  • The speed gives way. Along the blue curve the momentum keeps rising while v creeps toward the amber line without reaching it.
  • The plot stops at p/c = 10. For m₀ = 1.0 the curve leaves the top at v = 0.995c, and the sim draws an arrow and "p → ∞".
  • At the slider's top, v = 0.999c, p/c is already 22.3 for m₀ = 1.0: more than twice the height of the plot.
Key idea. Near c, speed barely changes while momentum keeps growing. The two are no longer proportional.
See itTake your point to v = 0.999c. Watch for: the marker leaving the top of the plot, with an arrow and "p → ∞" in its place.
04

γ is always there, but easy to miss at low speed

The blue curve is Newton's m₀v multiplied by the Lorentz factor γ, at every speed. Nothing switches on at some threshold.

The sim's axes show p/c = γ m₀ β.
  • At v = 0.1c, γ = 1.005: a 0.5% change. That is the right edge of the low-velocity view, where blue and grey look like one line.
  • The ratio layer shades p − m₀v, the momentum that γ adds. At v = 0.9c and m₀ = 1.0, p/c = 2.06 against Newton's 0.90, so the band, 1.16, is taller than Newton's whole value.
See itZoom into the low-velocity view at v = 0.05c. Watch for: the blue curve lying on top of the grey dashed line.
See itSwitch the ratio layer on at v = 0.9c. Watch for: the shaded band between the grey line and the blue curve, taller than the grey line's own height.
05

How steeply momentum climbs

Momentum grows faster than speed, and the gap widens as v approaches c. Values for m₀ = 1.0:

speed vγp/cNewton m₀v
0.45c1.120.5040.450
0.90c2.292.060.900
0.99c7.097.020.990
0.999c22.422.30.999
  • Doubling v from 0.45c to 0.90c multiplies p by 4.10. Newton gives 2.
  • From 0.90c to 0.99c, v rises by 10% while p rises by a factor of 3.4. From 0.99c to 0.999c, v rises by 0.9% and p by a factor of 3.2.
See itDouble the speed from 0.45c to 0.90c. Watch for: the card reporting p/c at each speed, and the factor between them.
06

What the rest mass does

Rest mass m₀ is a property of the particle, the same number in every frame. In p/c = γ m₀ β it multiplies everything, and γ contains no mass.

m₀ v

These sliders move the sim too.

  • Doubling m₀ doubles p at every speed. At v = 0.6c, p/c is 0.750 for m₀ = 1.0 and 1.50 for m₀ = 2.0.
  • The speed limit stays at c, and γ does not change.
  • The curve reaches the top of the fixed axis at a lower speed (0.995c for m₀ = 1.0, 0.981c for m₀ = 2.0), only because every value is larger.
See itCompare m₀ = 1.0 with m₀ = 2.0 at v = 0.6c. Watch for: p/c doubling from 0.750 to 1.50 while γ stays at 1.25.
07

Why γ is forced, and what stays fixed

Total momentum has to be conserved in a collision in every inertial frame. Velocities do not simply add between frames, so a collision that conserves Σ m₀v in one frame generally does not conserve it in a boosted frame. Σ γ m₀ v, together with the total energy, is conserved in every inertial frame. That is why γ belongs in the definition, and is not a fit to data. (The sim does not simulate collisions. This is the argument behind the curve.)

Energy and momentum together form one four-vector, with E = γ m₀c². With the course's metric (η₀₀ = −1, ηij = δij), its length is the same in every frame:

In other frames p and E change, but m₀ does not. Moving the m₀ slider changes the particle, not the frame. Rearranged, the length is:

Check. At m₀ = 1.0 and v = 0.6c: E/c² = γm₀ = 1.25 and p/c = 0.750, and 1.25² − 0.750² = 1 = m₀².
See itSet Lecture 14's particle: m₀ = 1.0 at v = 0.6c. Watch for: the readout γ = 1.25, p/c = 0.750, the space part of pμ = (1.25, 0.75, 0, 0) m₀c.
08

Where it matters

  • Magnetic spectrometers. A charge q moving across a field B follows a circle of radius r = p/(qB), with p = γ m₀ v. Detectors measure momentum from the curvature of the track.
  • The LHC. A 6.8 TeV proton has γ = E/(m₀c²) ≈ 7250, so its speed is within about 10⁻⁸ of c. The speed tells almost nothing, which is why beams are quoted in TeV and not in m/s.
Go deeper: low speed, and "relativistic mass"
  • Low speed. For v ≪ c, γ ≈ 1 + ½β², so p ≈ m₀v (1 + ½v²/c²). At 0.1c the correction is 0.5%, the size of γ − 1 in the low-velocity view.
  • One mass. Some older texts write p = m(v) v with m = γm₀ and call it "relativistic mass". This course keeps one mass, the invariant m₀. γ goes with the velocity, and not with the mass.
09

Summary

In one line. Relativistic momentum is p = γ m₀ v. Speed is capped at c, but momentum has no ceiling, because γ grows without limit as v approaches c.

Key points

  • At low speed γ ≈ 1, and p matches Newton's m₀v.
  • The rest mass multiplies the whole curve. γ carries no mass.
  • γ is forced by conservation in every frame. With energy it makes a four-vector whose length, −m₀²c², is invariant.
  • Near c, momentum (or energy) is the useful measure, not speed.

Common mix-ups

  • "Momentum levels off near c." The speed levels off. p = γ m₀ v keeps growing; the 0–10 axis is where the plot stops, not where the physics does.
  • "γ already carries the mass, so m₀ doesn't matter." γ = 1/√(1 − β²) contains no mass. Doubling m₀ doubles every p and leaves the speed limit at c.
  • "Mass grows with speed, so m₀ is the wrong mass." The course uses one mass, the rest (invariant) mass. γ goes with the velocity.

Things to try on your own

  • With m₀ = 1.0, find the speed at which p/c = 1.00, and compare it with Newton's.
  • Set m₀ = 5.0 and find the speed at which the marker leaves the plot. Compare it with 0.995c for m₀ = 1.0.
  • Turn the ratio layer on and find the speed above which the band is taller than the grey line at the same speed.
